# Two-Machine Split Workday and Closeout (2026-09-24)

On 2026-09-24 the working day was deliberately split across two machines — Windows during the day, Mac in the evening — and closed out from the Windows laptop with a structured sign-off: push every context repo, consolidate Tier A memory under its character cap, and write a handoff of record naming everything the Mac still owed. The day also carried an S2 data migration to Google Drive and eight merged PRs. The handoff lives at `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\global-memory\handoffs\2026-09-24-machine-split.md`.

## Key Points

- **Unpushed work blocks sign-off.** Four context repos — `global-memory`, `dotclaude`, `claude-memory-compiler`, and `SecondBrain` — were committed and pushed even though three carried changes left behind by *other* sessions. Rather than leaving them dirty or deferring, the closeout named the foreign changes explicitly in its report and pushed them.
- **Tier A memory is consolidated by displacement, not growth.** `MEMORY.md` sits under a 2,500-character cap; adding a "Machine split (9/24)" line required removing the existing "Data pulls" line, landing the file at 2,378 characters. A capped memory file forces an explicit eviction decision on every addition.
- **Cross-machine delegation is unverifiable from the delegating side.** Instructions sent to a Mac session cannot report back, so every Mac-side item is recorded as "unconfirmed" until the user verifies on that machine — including a backup plist moved to 21:00, to be checked with `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.dailybackup | grep -A4 -i calendar`.
- **The handoff enumerates per-machine next actions, not a merged list.** Windows: run `ritual-check.ps1 -Notify` once, then `Enable-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'KeystoneOS-Rituals'`. Mac: rsync `ol_scores.csv` and `team_scores.csv` from `~/DEV/S2_Evaluation/data/` to the Drive S2 folder, `launchctl bootout …/com.keystone.rituals`, and a first `export_snapshot.py` run in each of three pull repos.
- **Open decisions and known failures were carried forward rather than silently dropped:** whether to add a Windows 17:30 auto-push of the context repos; fixing the failing "Backup AI Sessions to Drive" task via `/claude-stack-doctor`; and pointing Perch's Windows reads at the Parquet snapshots.

## Details

The closeout's governing rule is that durable state must be durable on *both* machines before the day is declared finished, which makes pushing the context repos non-negotiable. This produced a deliberate reversal of the earlier practice of deferring commits in a dirty tree: three of the four repos held work authored by other concurrent sessions, and the choice was to commit and push them anyway while naming each foreign change in the report. The reasoning is that the alternative — leaving them dirty — guarantees the next session on either machine inherits an ambiguous working tree, whereas pushing with attribution costs only a slightly noisier history. The transparency step (naming whose change went along for the ride) is what makes the blanket push defensible; see [[concepts/scoped-commit-in-dirty-working-tree]] for the scoped-commit discipline this consciously departs from and the four-day deferral cost that motivated the change.

The machine split also exposes a structural asymmetry: the Windows session can *issue* work to the Mac but cannot *observe* it. Every Mac-side item therefore enters the handoff in an unconfirmed state with an explicit verification command attached, so the user — the only agent present on both machines — can close the loop. The same asymmetry appeared within the Windows session itself when a direct check of the S2 Drive folder was refused by the permission layer (see [[concepts/athlete-data-permission-block]]) and when a background watch on that folder was reaped under memory pressure (see [[concepts/background-job-reaped-memory-pressure]]); in all three cases the honest output is a named gap rather than an assumed success. The cross-machine data plumbing being established — `export_snapshot.py` in each pull repo producing Parquet snapshots that the other machine reads — is the structural answer to this: rather than each host reaching into the other's live data, both read committed snapshots, which is also why Perch's Windows reads are queued to be repointed at them.

# Claude Code Three-Tier Memory Architecture

The Claude Code memory system is composed of three independent layers, each operating at a different granularity and owned by a different mechanism. This architecture was articulated on 2026-05-19 during a session that traced exactly when and how each capture mechanism fires, and clarified several non-obvious details about hook timing and agent visibility. On 2026-06-05, a practical capacity-management routing pattern emerged for when Tier B global memory approaches its character cap.

## Key Points

- **Tier A — Native Claude Code auto-memory:** Built into Claude Code itself; managed per-project; no user configuration required. Operates automatically within a project context; its exact retention and synthesis mechanics are not user-visible.
- **Tier B — Custom global scratchpad via Stop hook:** A user-configured hook on the `Stop` event, which fires after every conversation turn. This provides incremental, per-turn transcript capture to a global scratchpad file (MEMORY.md) — a granularity that neither Tier A nor Tier C provides.
- **Tier C — claude-memory-compiler:** The [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] system: `SessionEnd` and `PreCompact` hooks fire shell commands at session teardown or auto-compaction, spawning a detached `flush.py` process that appends structured notes to the daily log; at end-of-day these are compiled into knowledge articles.
- **The agent never sees a "session ending" event.** Session end and compaction are harness-level events; it is the Claude Code harness that runs the hook shell commands, not the agent itself. This means an in-context agent cannot intercept or react to its own termination — only the hooks can.
- **PreCompact as a safety net:** In a long session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one. If a session later crashes before `SessionEnd` fires, at least one Tier C log was written at the most recent compaction — preventing total context loss.
- **When Tier B is near cap, route to Tier A project files:** The global MEMORY.md (Tier B) has a character-cap constraint. When it approaches capacity, new durable facts should be saved to Tier A project-specific memory files (e.g., `project_<name>.md`, `user_career_timeline.md`) rather than forcing compression of existing Tier B entries. Tier A project files are cross-project searchable via memsearch — they are not siloed to a single project context.

## Details

The three tiers are designed to capture context at different time horizons and granularities, and they operate independently rather than hierarchically. Tier A is fully opaque to the user — Claude Code manages it internally on a per-project basis. Tier B's Stop-hook scratchpad is the most granular: because the Stop event fires after every conversation turn, Tier B can capture mid-session context incrementally in near-real-time. This is especially useful for long sessions where intermediate turns might be compacted away before Tier C's end-of-session capture fires. Tier C produces the richest synthesized output — compiled knowledge articles from daily logs — but fires only at session boundaries.

The independence of the three tiers is their key reliability property. A failure in one does not cascade to the others: if a session crashes before `SessionEnd` fires (blocking Tier C's flush), the Stop-hook's Tier B scratchpad may still contain the session's important turns. If the Stop hook misfires, Tier A's native memory and Tier C's PreCompact-triggered captures are unaffected. The "agent never sees session ending" detail is architecturally important for anyone building on top of these hooks: code written inside the agent context cannot detect or react to its own session ending. Teardown logic must be placed in hook shell commands that the harness executes, not in agent-side instructions. This distinction separates what the LLM can do (respond to turns, use tools) from what the harness can do (run shell commands on system events like session end, compaction, or turn completion).

The Tier B near-cap routing pattern (2026-06-05) addresses a practical capacity constraint that emerges over time as the global MEMORY.md accumulates active threads. The USER.md profile has a hard 1,375-character cap (documented in [[concepts/end-of-day-structured-interview]]), and MEMORY.md's Tier B can similarly fill as a productive user's open questions and active threads accumulate across weeks. The correct response when Tier B is near capacity is not to compress existing entries — which risks discarding information encoded in current phrasing — but to route new durable facts into named Tier A project memory files. These files are typically named per relationship or project (e.g., `project_kenny_boyd.md` for facts about a key stakeholder, `user_career_timeline.md` for career-context facts that help future sessions orient quickly) but are surfaced by memsearch across all project contexts. Routing to Tier A therefore sacrifices no cross-project retrievability while relieving pressure on the shared Tier B capacity. Facts that belong in Tier A project files are those that are both durable (will not become stale quickly) and specific enough that they do not need to live in the global scope — as opposed to cross-cutting facts about user preferences or universal workflow patterns that genuinely belong in Tier B's global scope.

# $dev-sync Repo Sweep (2026-09-23 Clean Run)

`$dev-sync` is a Codex-invoked sweep that walks every repository under `Desktop\DEV`, pushes local commits, pulls incoming ones, and reports anomalies. The 2026-09-23 run was accepted as clean: 143 repos checked and pushed, 3 pulled incoming commits, none cloned or created, and no `.from-*` conflict files generated. It is the routine counterpart to the one-time staged migration described in [[concepts/dev-github-drive-migration-policy]] — the mechanism that keeps the migrated estate synchronized afterward.

## Key Points

- **Clean-run signature:** 143 repos checked and pushed, 3 with incoming commits pulled, 0 cloned or created, 0 `.from-*` conflict files. The absence of `.from-*` files is the sweep's primary conflict indicator — their presence means a two-machine divergence needed manual reconciliation.
- **Known benign exception:** `AthleticMedicineReviews` remains an empty unversioned folder and is expected to appear as such; a recurring non-defect that would otherwise read as a miss on every run.
- **The sweep feeds work selection.** With sync clean, the session picked up `PFF_Data_Project` per its `STATUS.md`: 2026 data covers graded weeks 0–3, the Parquet exchange is complete on both machines, nothing blocking. Per-repo `STATUS.md` files act as the resumable queue.
- **Sync health is reported separately from repo health.** The same day's `daily-backup` reported `repo-behind-blocked:global-memory` and the memory compiler had 2 pending logs plus a stale compile lock reclaimed after 1531 minutes (~25.5 h) — failures in the automation layer that a clean DEV sweep does not cover.

## Details

The value of a sweep like `$dev-sync` is that it converts a 143-repo estate from something no one can hold in mind into a single pass/fail signal with a small set of named exceptions. Its output is only meaningful if the expected exceptions are documented — `AthleticMedicineReviews` as a permanently empty unversioned folder is exactly such a case, and recording it prevents a recurring benign finding from either being re-investigated each run or, worse, training the reader to ignore the anomaly section entirely. The `.from-*` conflict-file convention gives the sweep a cheap divergence detector: rather than attempting a merge across two machines, it materializes the incoming variant under a suffixed name and leaves reconciliation to a human, so "no `.from-*` files" is a positive statement that no repo diverged, not merely that no push failed.

The session's second observation is that a clean sweep in one layer says nothing about adjacent automation. The `daily-backup` job reported `repo-behind-blocked:global-memory` — the backup declining to proceed because that repo was behind its remote — and the memory compiler had accumulated 2 pending logs behind a compile lock held for 1531 minutes before being reclaimed. A lock held over a day indicates a crashed or killed holder rather than legitimate contention, and the reclamation is the recovery path; the pending-log backlog is the visible cost. This is the same class of scheduled-job drift catalogued in [[concepts/automation-stack-doctor]], where periodic health-check runs surface exactly these per-task escalations, and it reinforces that "sync is clean" and "the automation stack is healthy" are independent claims requiring independent checks.

- [[concepts/automation-stack-doctor]] — The consolidated health check covering the scheduled tasks and error-log escalations (`repo-behind-blocked`, stale compile lock) that this sync run surfaced but does not itself remediate.

# Memsearch: Setup, Python Migration Recovery, and Indexing

Memsearch is a local semantic search tool that indexes Claude Code's Tier A project-memory files, enabling cross-project retrieval of durable knowledge without directly accessing each project's files. On 2026-06-11, memsearch indexing failures were diagnosed and resolved: the root cause was a Python migration that left a hardcoded stale path inside memsearch.exe, making it unable to locate its runtime. Recovery required reinstalling memsearch into the new Python environment, re-applying the flush patch, and replacing the stale shim. After recovery, 805 chunks were confirmed indexed and searchable. On 2026-06-13, a concurrent-contention ETIMEDOUT pattern was observed and characterized. On 2026-06-17, the same Python-path-capture failure class was confirmed in a second tool. On 2026-07-27, a recurring indexing alarm was correctly re-diagnosed as structural — a first-time embedding index is an hours-scale job — and the reindex was relocated from the session-end hook to a nightly scheduled task.

## Key Points

- **Cross-project Tier A search:** Tier A project-memory files (see [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]]) are cross-project searchable via memsearch — not siloed to a single project context. Future sessions can surface facts from `project_<name>.md` and `user_career_timeline.md` files regardless of which project they are working in.
- **Python migration breaks memsearch:** memsearch.exe embeds a path to the Python executable at install time (hardcoded shebang or binary-embedded interpreter path). When Python is migrated — old installation deleted, new one installed at a different path — memsearch fails because its embedded path is no longer valid. The failure is an install-time path capture becoming stale, not a configuration issue.
- **Recovery sequence (three steps):**
  1. Reinstall memsearch into the new Python environment so the new Python path is embedded in the binary
  2. Re-apply the flush patch (a memsearch modification enabling integration with Claude Code's Stop hook)
  3. Replace the stale shim file with one pointing to the new installation
- **After recovery on 2026-06-11:** 805 chunks indexed and confirmed searchable.
- **`index` command requires explicit paths:** memsearch's `index` command does not auto-discover project memory directories; the hook or invocation script must pass explicit file and directory paths. Implicit discovery is not supported — the explicit-paths requirement makes indexing scope deterministic and auditable.
- **ETIMEDOUT concurrent contention (2026-06-13):** when multiple Claude Code sessions or background jobs invoke memsearch near-simultaneously, they contend for the same index and produce ETIMEDOUT errors. On 2026-06-13, 6 ETIMEDOUTs were logged over 24 hours, with 3 occurring within 1.2 seconds of each other at 13:40. Timeouts are non-fatal by design — they do not corrupt the index; subsequent invocations succeed once contention clears.
- **Silent `exit 1` (2026-06-13):** a separate failure class from ETIMEDOUTs; one silent `exit 1` with no surviving diagnostic output was observed. The cause is unknown. This failure class is harder to diagnose because no error text is preserved; if recurring, it warrants adding stderr capture to the hook script.
- **Python path-capture staleness affects standard venvs too (2026-06-17):** the same failure class that breaks memsearch.exe also affects standard Python `.venv` environments. The `morning-briefing` pipeline's `.venv` was broken from 2026-06-12 because its `pyvenv.cfg` referenced `C:\Python314`, which no longer existed after a Python version migration. The fix is identical in structure: rebuild the venv against the current Python.
- **First-time index is hours-scale and structural (2026-07-27):** a recurring session-end indexing alarm, previously misdiagnosed as an "occasional" hiccup, was recognized as structural — a first-time SecondBrain book-library embedding job runs for hours (one indexer had burned 81 CPU-minutes and was still going). A 45-second session-end hook can never absorb an hours-scale index.
- **Reindex relocated to a nightly scheduled task (2026-07-27):** the heavy reindex was moved into the 6:15 AM `daily-backup.ps1` backup task — uncapped, using the full `memsearch.exe` path, escalating per-path failures, and resetting the hook timeout-streak counter on success. The session-end hook stays a light 45-second incremental pass, and its alarm threshold was raised 3→6 so it only fires when the nightly safety net itself falls behind. The library index converges over a night or two while search stays live.

## Details

The Python shebang path problem in memsearch represents a distinct class of tool-configuration staleness from environment-variable and PATH issues. Unlike `setx` propagation failures (where a new value is written to the registry but not yet visible in running processes — see [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]]) or Task Scheduler PATH omissions (where the system spawns a process without the user's PATH — see [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]]), the memsearch issue lives in the tool's own binary: a specific file path was captured at install time and embedded in the executable. When that path ceases to exist, the binary fails at startup regardless of what the current environment looks like. The diagnostic fingerprint is: `memsearch.exe` appears to exist, its location is on PATH, but running it produces errors about Python or interpreter paths. The correct remediation is reinstallation — not PATH configuration or environment variable adjustment — because the problem is inside the binary, not in the environment surrounding it.

The flush patch is a memsearch modification specific to the Claude Code integration: it wires memsearch into the Stop hook workflow so that each conversation turn's memory captures are immediately indexed as new chunks without requiring a manual re-index command. The patch must be re-applied after any reinstallation because reinstalling memsearch produces a fresh, unmodified binary. The durable practice for maintaining patched tools is: (1) document the patch in a known location so it is not forgotten, (2) reinstall cleanly, (3) re-apply the documented patch. The 805-chunk count after recovery confirms all previously-indexed Tier A files were successfully re-ingested — a full re-index (rather than an incremental one) is the safest recovery approach.

The 2026-06-13 ETIMEDOUT contention pattern reflects an architectural constraint: memsearch maintains an exclusive lock on its index file during writes. When multiple concurrent Claude Code sessions — or the primary session plus background jobs like the memory-compiler flush — all attempt to write to the index within the same narrow window, lock contention produces ETIMEDOUTs in the losing processes. Because the failures are non-fatal by design, occasional contention under normal multi-session usage is acceptable. If the rate increases significantly, the mitigation is to stagger memsearch-dependent hooks using a random jitter or backoff strategy.

The 2026-06-17 morning-briefing venv failure generalizes the Python path-capture staleness to a broader class. Both memsearch.exe (compiled binary with embedded interpreter path) and a standard `.venv` (directory with `pyvenv.cfg` containing `home = C:\Python314`) become non-functional when `C:\Python314` is removed. The detection pattern is the same — the tool appears to exist but fails to start, with error messages referencing a Python path that no longer exists — and the fix is the same: rebuild the environment against the current Python installation.

The 2026-07-27 finding corrects a diagnostic error and produces an architectural fix. The recurring memsearch indexing alarm had been dismissed the prior day as an occasional hiccup; in fact it was structural — the first-time embedding index for the SecondBrain book library is an hours-scale job, evidenced by one indexer consuming 81 CPU-minutes without completing. A 45-second session-end hook cannot possibly finish such a job, and attempts to run it as an in-session background command were killed with the session (see [[concepts/in-session-background-process-limits]]). The fix relocated the heavy reindex into the nightly 6:15 AM `daily-backup.ps1` scheduled task, which runs uncapped (its execution limit widened to 2 hours), uses the full `memsearch.exe` path per the Task Scheduler minimal-PATH constraint, escalates per-path failures to `.errors.log`, and resets the hook timeout-streak counter on success. With the heavy work on a nightly cadence, the session-end hook is left as a light 45-second incremental pass and its consecutive-miss alarm threshold is raised from 3 to 6 — the alarm now fires only if the nightly safety net itself falls behind, making it a real signal instead of chronic noise. The full library index converges over a night or two while incremental search stays live throughout.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] — The three-tier memory architecture that memsearch serves: Tier A project-specific files are cross-project searchable via memsearch, and the explicit-paths requirement in the `index` command determines which Tier A files are indexed.
- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — The broader discipline of maintaining Claude Code's tooling environment; the memsearch reinstall and reindex relocation are maintenance operations in the same class.
- [[concepts/automation-stack-doctor]] — The 2026-07-27 session that relocated the hours-scale reindex into the nightly backup task and raised the session-end alarm threshold 3→6; the stack doctor monitors memsearch health as one of its checks.
- [[concepts/in-session-background-process-limits]] — Explains why the hours-scale reindex could not run as an in-session background command (killed with the session) and had to move to a scheduled job.
- [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]] — The nightly reindex task uses the full `memsearch.exe` path per this Task Scheduler minimal-PATH lesson.
- [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]] — A related class of tool-configuration staleness where a value is captured at a point in time and does not update when the system changes.

# Project Triage and Retrospective Methodology

On 2026-05-21, a structured 7-day retrospective (covering May 14–21) and a cold-project triage exercise were conducted to address project sprawl across many concurrent initiatives. The retrospective produced a structured cross-project summary of work completed and 7 open loops with next actions; the triage sorted cold projects into 4 buckets and shipped a decision-tracking HTML artifact at `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html`.

## Key Points

- **7-day retrospective format:** a structured recap of all projects touched in a rolling window, categorized by status, covering CLI development (Zotero, Catapult), 5 new skills installed, Fireflies setup, memory and Obsidian integration, token dashboard setup, and side fixes for May 14–21. Concluded with 7 identified open loops, each paired with a concrete next action.
- **Cold-project 4-bucket triage:** cold projects (not touched during the retrospective window) are sorted into: **Resume** (active work, blocked on a specific next action), **Decide** (uncertain whether to continue; needs a deliberate go/no-go decision), **Done** (formally closeable), **Archive/Kill** (permanently deprioritized or abandoned). The 2026-05-21 run sorted 16 projects: 3 resume, 2 decide, 3 done, 8 archive/kill.
- **Triage output artifact:** `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html` — a self-contained HTML file summarizing all bucketed projects with statuses and next actions, usable offline without re-running the triage.
- **Hottest cold project:** `Risk_Stratification_Engine` was flagged as the highest-priority cold project to resume next.
- **Project sprawl as a recurring pattern:** the user explicitly noted difficulty maintaining orientation across many concurrent initiatives; periodic retrospectives and triage dashboards were identified as the structural remedy.

## Details

The retrospective was triggered by the user explicitly losing track of what had been started, stopped, or left mid-flight — a common failure mode when many parallel workstreams run simultaneously across different tools, repositories, and roles. Rather than relying on memory or ad-hoc review, the session generated a structured cross-project summary covering the prior 7 days, making the "what exists and where it stands" question answerable in a single, deliberate pass. The format mirrors a lightweight sprint retrospective: scope (what was touched), status (done vs. in-flight vs. blocked), and open loops (concrete next actions, not vague intentions).

The 4-bucket triage model is designed to force explicit decisions rather than letting cold projects accumulate indefinitely in an ambiguous "maybe later" state. **Resume** identifies projects with a clear next action that are still worth pursuing. **Decide** surfaces projects that need a deliberate go/no-go call rather than being quietly ignored — the act of naming these forces a decision that passive neglect defers indefinitely. **Done** provides a formal closure signal for work that is genuinely complete but hasn't been officially closed. **Archive/Kill** handles deliberate deprioritization — not forgotten, but explicitly moved out of active consideration. The HTML artifact makes the triage durable and reviewable without accessing the session that produced it; sharing it as a file also separates the "what was triaged" question from the "what should I do next" question, allowing the artifact to be reviewed asynchronously.

The retrospective also surfaced a secondary benefit: completing deferred follow-up work from prior sessions. Specifically, the Zotero CLI's `sync --full` verification — left pending after the v0.1 slash command was registered on 2026-05-19 — was completed during the retrospective, with 2,064 items ingested successfully in ~75 seconds. Catching and completing loose ends like this is a natural output of a structured retrospective: open loops that were "almost done" become clearly visible and easy to close within the retrospective session itself.

# Telemetry Export Automation via Browser Driving (telemetry_pull.py)

On 2026-09-29, after shipping PP_Recruiting workbook 015, work began on `scripts/telemetry_pull.py` — a Playwright-driven tool to automate the 22-file manual export routine that feeds the recruiting workbooks from Teamworks Telemetry. Browser automation was chosen over two rejected alternatives: a printing-press-generated API CLI (blocked by the project's own handoff rules) and the paid Teamworks API. On 2026-09-30 the tool was repaired rather than rebuilt — a scope-filter defect was fixed and pushed as `20e2de6` — and it then carried the 2023, 2024, and 2026 leaderboard pulls, including a clean 44-file 2026 load.

## Key Points

- **The API route was ruled out on policy, not capability.** The printing-press skill generates CLIs from API specs, and PP_Recruiting's handoff Rule 3 forbids touching Telemetry's auth token or internal API; the sanctioned alternative, the Teamworks API, costs money. Browser automation was the remaining option, and the 2026-09-30 session re-confirmed that the Player Traits and Advanced Stats leaderboard pages are exactly what the tool already downloads, so no new CLI was warranted.
- **Read the filter pills individually, not the wrapper.** Telemetry changed its filter box; the original code read the wrapper element, so a two-pill state came back as the single string `"Power FourFBS"`. Reading each pill separately is what makes scope assertions meaningful.
- **Additions must precede removals.** The site refuses to remove the last remaining filter pill, so `set_scope` was reordered to add FBS *before* removing Power Four. A naive "clear then set" sequence deadlocks on this rule — the same reason the "Clear" control never removed Power Four scope in the first place.
- **A hidden Chrome window is a silent download stall.** When `document.hidden` is true, screenshots freeze and CSV downloads stop after the first file — observed on 9/16 and again on 9/30, resolved both times by bringing the window forward. Three runs where Chrome exited with code 0 mid-download were attributed to the window being closed or a pending Chrome self-update, not a crash; the operating rule is to leave the tool's Chrome window alone for roughly five minutes during a run and to check for a pending "Relaunch to update" beforehand.
- **Design is defensive by construction:** elements are located by label rather than position, each downloaded file is validated (correct tab, group, row count, not a duplicate of the previous file), a manifest is written at the end, filenames follow the 2025 convention, and nothing is overwritten. The QB test file was deliberately deleted before the full run so the manifest would list every file produced by that run.
- **The position-group selector is searchable** (type, select, verify), which makes the 11-group loop reliable once the first two downloads succeed; scope and season still reset to Power Four / 2026 on every switch between the Player Traits and Advanced Stats tabs and must be re-set and re-verified per tab batch.

## Details

The decision path is the notable part: a request for a generated CLI was declined on grounds internal to the project rather than on technical grounds. The printing-press workflow builds CLIs from API specifications, so satisfying it would have required inspecting Telemetry's auth token and internal API — exactly what the project's handoff Rule 3 prohibits. With the documented alternative behind a paywall, browser automation became the choice by elimination. The 2026-09-30 repair extends that reasoning into maintenance: when the vendor changed its filter markup, the response was a targeted fix to scope handling plus a commit and push, not a rewrite. A UI-driven integration has no contract, so its failures arrive as markup changes, and the maintenance posture that follows is small localized repairs against observed breakage.

Both defects fixed on 9/30 are characteristic of automating a UI. The wrapper-vs-pill bug produced a *plausible-looking* scope string (`"Power FourFBS"`) that no assertion rejected, which is the exact failure the per-file validation exists to catch; the fix was to read the underlying individual elements rather than their container — stepping down from a convenient aggregate to the ground-truth elements. The add-before-remove ordering is a constraint of the site's own filter semantics (it will not drop to zero pills), so the automation has to encode an ordering a human operator would have discovered by trial. The Chrome-visibility findings are the most operationally important, because they make the automation's failure mode a *partial* success: the first file downloads, subsequent ones silently do not, and Chrome may exit cleanly with status 0. An exit code of 0 after an incomplete batch is therefore not evidence of success, and the manifest plus row-count checks are the only reliable completion signal — a local instance of reconciling a reported exit status against on-disk artifacts.

Validation against live data followed a graduated escalation: a QB Player Traits 2026 FBS test returned 264 rows from 138 teams, then the full pull ran. The 2023 and 2024 baseline pulls produced 44 verified files (133 teams in 2023, 134 in 2024), filed via `file_exports.py` into `_exports/2023_baseline/fbs/` and `_exports/2024_baseline/fbs/`, and the full 2026 load (FBS plus FCS and Group of Six) ran clean at 14,397 players with 1,485 flagged players meeting the snap minimum. Export scope was standardized to FBS with a Minimum Snaps 1 filter to match the 2025 exports. # PP_Recruiting Three-Season Honors Benchmark (2023–2025)

On 2026-09-30 the PP_Recruiting honors benchmark was extended from a single 2025 season to three seasons (2023–2025) by pulling 2023 and 2024 Telemetry leaderboard exports and re-running the honors matcher. The result is 1,417 honoree player-seasons — roughly double the prior 710 — with 1,679 of 1,681 honors matched (99.9%), written to `_exports/honors/honors_benchmark_2023_2025.csv`. The expanded reference population was then placed *beside* the existing workbook 013 targets rather than replacing them, and immediately exposed several targets sitting well above what actual honorees achieve.

## Key Points

- **Scale and match rate:** 1,417 honoree player-seasons across 2023–2025 (from 710), 1,679/1,681 honors matched. The two misses were Justin Lockhart (San José State 2023, absent from Telemetry's 2023 export) and a duplicate Dylan Sampson row — a near-complete match rate whose residual is attributable to source gaps rather than matcher logic.
- **Telemetry's Team column is the season's school, not the current one.** Verified via Cam Ward 2023 → Washington State and Will Howard 2023 → Kansas State. This makes multi-season joins safe without transfer-portal correction.
- **Medians sit beside targets, not in place of them.** The user's explicit call was to show honoree medians side by side with 013's targets, preserving the existing rubric so any divergence is attributable to the reference population rather than to a changed threshold.
- **Several 013 targets exceed honoree medians,** including OT Pass Blocking 79 vs median 67, OT Stops Allowed 65 vs 41, OG Penalty 71 vs 50.5, EDGE Disruption 80 vs 65, and CB CROE 74 vs 65. Because the targets were derived from Player Impact 90+ players, either that group over-sets the bar or those metrics simply do not track honors.
- **Sample thinness bounds the conclusions:** the All-American population is too small at QB (7) and TE (6) to support per-position inference, so the benchmark is read as position-conditional and not uniformly trustworthy.
- **Defaults were set by the agent and flagged as changeable:** minimum snaps 300, and second-team All-Americans sourced from AP only. Four metric renames were applied in the build script so names match PORTAL INPUT (e.g. `EPA/Target` → `EPA Per Target`) and the SETTINGS lookups line up.

## Details

The benchmark's analytical value comes entirely from widening the reference population: with one season, a target above the honoree median could be dismissed as noise; with three seasons and 1,417 player-seasons, a target 24 points above the honoree median on OT Stops Allowed is a property of the rubric rather than of the sample. The deliberate decision to show medians *alongside* the existing targets — rather than overwriting them — is what makes that comparison legible to the people who own the thresholds, and it mirrors the discipline used in the earlier benchmark workbook, where no formula or threshold was altered so that any difference between versions was attributable to population alone. The consequence is a question that the data can frame but not settle: whether the Player Impact 90+ cohort used to derive the targets represents a genuinely higher bar than award voters apply, or whether the flagged metrics (offensive-line pass blocking and penalties, EDGE disruption, CB CROE) simply have no relationship to honors selection. That question was explicitly deferred to a conversation rather than resolved by edit.

Two methodological details matter for anyone re-running the build. First, the Team-column semantics were verified rather than assumed: Telemetry records the school the player played for *in that season*, so a multi-year join needs no transfer reconciliation — a check worth making explicitly, since the opposite convention would have silently mis-assigned every transfer's honors. Second, the choices that the matcher cannot derive from data were set as named, changeable defaults (300-snap minimum, AP-only second-team All-Americans) and recorded as such, which keeps them visible for later revision instead of hardening into unexamined behavior. Metric renaming in the build script, rather than in the workbook, keeps the lookup contract with PORTAL INPUT and SETTINGS in one place.

The expanded benchmark also surfaced a downstream screening concern. After the full 2026 load, per-position flagged counts ran far above the 30–50 range the stakeholder wanted — offensive guard at 316 and offensive tackle at 175, with running back (48) the only position inside the range — attributed to the offensive-line profile route adding names. That is the same open concern as the target-versus-median gaps, seen from the output side: thresholds that no honoree clears cannot discriminate, and a board that returns 316 names at one position is not a shortlist.

# Honors Exclusion Rule: Key Granularity and Fail-Loud Guards

The PP_Recruiting honors matcher must decide whether an award counts as a position honor, and return-specialist selections filed under combined wiki-style headings repeatedly defeated that decision. Over 2026-09-30, three successive ship candidates were verified and two were blocked: workbook 016 failed because a return-only award still produced an All-America flag, 017 failed on provenance even though its numbers were correct, and 018 shipped only after the exclusion list was re-keyed to a single specific award and given a fail-loud guard.

## Key Points

- **Position-honor co-occurrence is not a sufficient proxy for an all-purpose selection.** The `keep_honor` rule admitted a combined all-purpose heading whenever the player also held a regular position honor that season; LaJohntay Wester's 2023 selection passed that test while the underlying awards were punt-returner selections — the exact category the rule was meant to exclude.
- **Combined headings cannot be trusted as the honor category.** The selector's own release (FWAA, Phil Steele, Sports Illustrated) names the specific role, so an "all-purpose / return specialist" heading in a secondary source must be resolved against the primary release rather than read as a category.
- **(season, source, player) was too coarse a key.** A player can hold both a return-specialist and a position honor in the same season from the same selector — Cooper DeJean held a 2023 Sports Illustrated kick-returner award *and* first-team All-America at defensive back — so heading and selectors had to join the key via a `return_role()` helper to drop the one award without dropping the legitimate one.
- **A hardcoded exclusion list needs a fail-loud guard.** `main()` exits with an error unless each exclusion entry matches exactly one raw award, so a shift in the raw data cannot silently under- or over-exclude. The guard was tightened to per-entry granularity on a reviewer's suggestion, and the rerun produced byte-identical outputs.
- **Numerically correct is not shippable.** Workbook 017 passed its arithmetic recompute (184 benchmark rows), its 40-cell 016→017 diff, and a SHA-256 match between the local and `Send\` copies, yet was blocked because the DeJean return-only award remained in the provenance trail, contradicting the A3 method note. The A3 note was ultimately rewritten so its wording matches the implemented rule.

## Details

The failures form a progression in which each fix exposed the next layer. The first rule tried to distinguish real all-purpose honorees from pure return specialists using a cheap signal — does the player also hold a position honor that season? — and Wester demonstrated that the signal is simply not the thing being asked about: holding a position honor says nothing about whether *this* award was a return award. Correcting that for Wester required naming the specific award, which then exposed the key-granularity problem through DeJean: an exclusion keyed on (season, source, player) would have removed his defensive-back All-America selection along with his kick-returner award, trading a false inclusion for a false exclusion. The resolution was to make the key as specific as the thing being excluded — season, source, normalized name, heading, and selectors — which is the general lesson: an exclusion list's key must have the same granularity as the unit it excludes, or it will inevitably over- or under-reach.

The fail-loud guard addresses the second structural weakness of hardcoded exclusions, which is that they are assertions about data that can change underneath them. An entry that silently stops matching produces an over-inclusive benchmark; one that starts matching extra rows produces an under-inclusive one; in both cases the numbers remain plausible and the defect is invisible. Requiring each entry to match exactly one raw award converts that silent drift into an immediate crash. The provenance block on 017 is the complementary lesson about artifacts: the A3 method note is a second, human-readable statement of the rule, and it does not update itself when the code does. Because the workbook ships to a stakeholder who will read the note rather than the code, a note that overstates the implemented rule is a real defect even when every cell is correct — so the note belongs on the re-verification checklist whenever the exclusion list changes. The arithmetic checks that all passed on 017 are precisely the checks that cannot catch this class of error; what caught both Wester and DeJean was a source-level check on each newly flagged player.

Operationally, the fixes were sequenced so that no shipped artifact was edited in place: 017 remains the copy going to the stakeholder (the Wester fix changed 40 All-American cells and all WR medians and counts), and 018 — which differs from 017 in exactly one cell, the A3 note, with every benchmark number byte-identical — will follow as a quiet replacement, after which 017 moves to `_to_delete/`. Superseded outputs were preserved under `_exports/honors/superseded_2026-09-30_v4/`.

# Read-Only, Low-Memory Verification Pass Protocol

Across 2026-09-30, three independent verification passes were run against PP_Recruiting ship candidates (workbooks 016, 017, and 018) under a fixed protocol: strictly read-only, memory-frugal, and driven by a written list of numbered checks. The protocol's two notable properties are that it never touches the artifact under review, and that its check list is written in a harness-agnostic form — which is what allowed a Sonnet 5.5 reviewer to complete the 018 pass verbatim after Codex hit its usage limit mid-run.

## Key Points

- **Read-only and memory-frugal by instruction:** Python's stdlib `csv` module instead of pandas, `openpyxl` opened with `read_only=True`, one workbook open at a time, and `scripts\check_workbook.py` explicitly off-limits. These constraints held across all three passes.
- **The check list is numbered and written down before the run.** The 018 pass enumerated six checks: exclusion-rule match scope plus the guard, input/output diffs against the prior version, workbook-to-workbook cell diff with an error-cell count and a spot check, whether the method note overstates the implemented rule, a SHA-256 match between the local copy and the `Send\` copy, and open-ended review of the changed parts.
- **Verdicts are binary and reported with a pass/fail table:** DO NOT SHIP 016, DO NOT SHIP 017, SHIP 018. Each report was written to a file (`codex_verification_v4.md`, `v5.md`, plus `docs/audits/` copies) rather than left in a transcript.
- **A written check list is portable across harnesses.** When Codex was rate-limited mid-verification, the queued retry was cancelled and a Sonnet 5.5 reviewer ran the same six checks, returning SHIP and one hardening suggestion that was applied. Writing checks harness-agnostically is what made the substitution cheap.
- **Verification defers to whichever session owns the artifact.** A second copy of the load and the checker were deliberately not run while a parallel PP_Recruiting session held Excel open; one session owned `STATUS.md` while the other wrote its own handoff file. A planned 016 checker run became moot when the parallel session had already produced 017.

## Details

The protocol's constraints exist because the thing being verified is simultaneously the thing being shipped. A read-only pass cannot accidentally become the fix, so a failed verdict leaves the artifact exactly as the stakeholder would receive it, and the SHA-256 comparison between the working copy and the staged `Send\` copy is meaningful rather than circular. The memory constraints are practical rather than stylistic: the audited workbooks are large, a parallel session frequently held Excel open, and loading an entire workbook into pandas alongside a live Excel instance is how a verification pass turns into a host-resource incident. Opening one workbook at a time with `read_only=True` and parsing CSVs with the stdlib reader keeps the pass cheap enough to repeat on every candidate — which is precisely what happened, three times in one day.

The harness-agnostic property of the check list is the transferable result. Because each check was written as a statement about the artifact ("the exclusion entries match only rows 627 and 629 and leave the DB row intact"; "018 differs from 017 only at HONORS BENCHMARK A3 with zero error cells") rather than as instructions to a particular tool, a rate-limited reviewer could be swapped for a different model without rewriting the work. The reviewer substitution also produced value beyond continuity: the replacement suggested a per-entry hardening of the guard, which was applied and confirmed to yield identical outputs. Treating a usage-limit interruption as a routing problem rather than a blocker depends entirely on the checks having been externalized first — the same reason the earlier, partially-completed audits were still worth having.

The concurrency discipline is the third element. With two sessions working the same project, the verification side declined to run anything that would contend for Excel or for `STATUS.md`, and recorded its findings in a separate handoff file instead. That cost one planned run (the 016 checker) becoming moot, which is the cheap outcome; the expensive outcome would have been two sessions writing the same status file or corrupting an open workbook.

# Box Access via Box Drive Desktop Sync (MCP and Connector Blocked)

On 2026-09-30, an attempt to give Claude Code access to Baylor Box through the Box MCP server failed and was abandoned in favor of the already-installed Box Drive desktop sync client. The MCP server at `https://mcp.box.com` rejects `claude mcp add` because it has no dynamic client registration and only accepts a Box OAuth app the user registers themselves; the self-registration path requires Baylor IT app approval, which Baylor blocks. The working route is the local folder `C:\Users\eric_rash\Box`, which behaves as an ordinary directory.

## Key Points

- **Box's MCP server requires a self-registered OAuth app.** It has no dynamic client registration, so `claude mcp add https://mcp.box.com` is rejected outright. The documented alternative is a Box Custom App with callback `http://localhost:8765/callback` plus `claude mcp add --client-id ... --callback-port 8765` — blocked at Baylor, and unblockable without IT app approval.
- **Remove a failed MCP entry rather than leaving it.** A broken server entry in user settings surfaces as a connection failure on *every* session start, so the entry was deleted. The claude.ai Box connector appeared in the list after `/reload-plugins` but remains unauthenticated and was left alone.
- **Box Drive desktop sync is the working route.** `C:\Users\eric_rash\Box` reads and writes like a normal folder and exposes `BU Athletics Performance Shared Drive`, `Kinexon`, `S2 Cognition 2026 Team Reports`, `WBB DATA`, and Fall Camp body-weight sheets.
- **The sync path is slow and feature-poor by comparison.** Files are cloud placeholders that download on first open, so large folders are slow; Box AI, shared links, collaborators, and Box metadata/tags are all unavailable through this route and need the API/MCP path.
- **The Box tree contains identifiable athlete health data** (e.g. `2025-12-15_InjuryTracking_Concussion.csv` and other injury/concussion tracking), to be handled with the same care as the DexaProject data: read locally, never pasted into chat, a published page, or an outside service.

## Details

This is a case where the blockage is institutional rather than technical, and the response differs accordingly. The vendor offers a sanctioned programmatic route, but exercising it requires registering an OAuth application inside the organization's Box tenant — a step only Baylor IT can approve, and which Baylor declines. Unlike a vendor-gated API where waiting on a contact may eventually succeed, or an internal prohibition that justifies driving the UI, here the capability exists and is simply withheld by policy, so the recorded decision is not to retry the MCP server or connector while the block stands. The fallback is not a workaround of the prohibition: Box Drive is an officially installed and supported client, and reading a synced folder is the same access the user already has at the filesystem level.

The trade-off is explicit. The filesystem route delivers the bulk of what was wanted — read, write, and analyze over the shared drives — but loses everything that lives above the file layer: Box AI, shared-link creation, collaborator management, and Box metadata/tags. It also has a performance characteristic worth planning around, since placeholder files hydrate on first open, making a first pass over a large folder substantially slower than a local one. Two operational notes generalize beyond Box: a failed MCP entry is not inert, because the harness retries it at every session start and surfaces the failure as recurring startup noise, so removal is the correct cleanup; and a convenient new filesystem mount can quietly widen the sensitive-data surface — the Box tree contains injury and concussion tracking with athlete identifiers, which places it under the same never-leaves-the-machine handling as other athlete health data in this environment.

# PP_Recruiting Workbook 015: HONORS BENCHMARK Tab

Workbook 015 of PP_Recruiting, adding a HONORS BENCHMARK tab, shipped on 2026-09-29. A Codex re-audit of it ran out of quota half-finished, having confirmed the Mountain West fix and all five selectors' second teams. The session also surfaced a substantive grading question: several SETTINGS targets sit well above the honoree medians the new tab exposes, suggesting the Profile REVIEW path may be over-filtering. On 2026-09-30 the lineage advanced three more numbers — 016 and 017 blocked or superseded on honors-inclusion defects, 018 verified SHIP — and the target-calibration question widened across four position groups.

## Key Points

- **The benchmark tab exposed a target-calibration problem, and the three-season benchmark widened it.** SETTINGS/013 targets sit above honoree medians at OT Pass Blocking (79 vs 67), OT Stops Allowed (65 vs 41), OG Penalty (71 vs 50.5), EDGE Disruption (80 vs 65), and CB CROE (74 vs 65) — raising the possibility that the Profile REVIEW path is over-filtering rather than identifying genuine concerns.

The next number is 019.

## Details

The HONORS BENCHMARK tab's value turned out to be diagnostic rather than merely descriptive: by putting honoree medians next to the configured targets, it made visible that some targets are set far above what actual honorees achieve. If a target exceeds what award-winning players at that position actually produce, then any player measured against it will fail, and the REVIEW flag it triggers carries no discriminating information. Extending the benchmark to three seasons sharpened this from a single suspicious metric into a pattern concentrated on the offensive line and on EDGE/CB disruption metrics, and the flagged-count distribution after the full 2026 load gave it an output-side confirmation: a position returning 316 names is not a shortlist, and the same offensive-line profile route implicated in those counts is where the target-versus-median gaps cluster. Notably, the resolution remains scoped as a judgment conversation with the position's owner rather than a unilateral threshold edit, and it stays paired with the still-pending 011 screening-matrix review because both ask where the flagging boundaries should sit.

The version discipline recorded here — a new number per correction, never an overwrite — treats a distributed workbook as immutable, and 2026-09-30 exercised it three times in one day. The two blocked candidates failed for different reasons: 016 on a substantive inclusion defect that changed cells, 017 on a provenance defect with no numerical effect at all. The handling of 018 shows how far the discipline extends: even a one-cell change to a method note becomes its own workbook number, shipped as a quiet replacement rather than patched into the copy already staged for the stakeholder. # Memsearch: Setup, Python Migration Recovery, and Indexing

Memsearch is a local semantic search tool that indexes Claude Code's Tier A project-memory files, enabling cross-project retrieval of durable knowledge without directly accessing each project's files. On 2026-06-11, memsearch indexing failures were diagnosed and resolved: the root cause was a Python migration that left a hardcoded stale path inside memsearch.exe, making it unable to locate its runtime. Recovery required reinstalling memsearch into the new Python environment, re-applying the flush patch, and replacing the stale shim. After recovery, 805 chunks were confirmed indexed and searchable. On 2026-06-13, a concurrent-contention ETIMEDOUT pattern was observed and characterized. On 2026-06-17, the same Python-path-capture failure class was confirmed in a second tool. On 2026-07-27, a recurring indexing alarm was correctly re-diagnosed as structural — a first-time embedding index is an hours-scale job — and the reindex was relocated from the session-end hook to a nightly scheduled task. On 2026-09-30, a further run of timeouts was traced to a stopped dependency rather than to memsearch itself.

## Key Points

- **Cross-project Tier A search:** Tier A project-memory files (see [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]]) are cross-project searchable via memsearch — not siloed to a single project context.
- **Python migration breaks memsearch:** memsearch.exe embeds a path to the Python executable at install time. When Python is migrated — old installation deleted, new one installed at a different path — memsearch fails because its embedded path is no longer valid. The failure is an install-time path capture becoming stale, not a configuration issue.
- **Recovery sequence (three steps):** reinstall memsearch into the new Python environment; re-apply the flush patch (the modification enabling Stop-hook integration); replace the stale shim file with one pointing to the new installation. After recovery on 2026-06-11, 805 chunks were indexed and confirmed searchable.
- **`index` command requires explicit paths:** memsearch's `index` command does not auto-discover project memory directories; the hook or invocation script must pass explicit file and directory paths, which makes indexing scope deterministic and auditable.
- **Timeouts have at least three distinct causes.** (1) *Concurrent contention* — multiple sessions or background jobs writing the same index produce non-fatal ETIMEDOUTs (6 in 24 hours on 2026-06-13, three within 1.2 seconds at 13:40); the index is not corrupted and later invocations succeed. (2) *Structural overrun* — a first-time embedding index is hours-scale and cannot fit a 45-second hook. (3) *A stopped dependency* — the timeouts logged across late September 2026 traced to Docker's Milvus container being down, not to broken memsearch code; the container was healthy roughly ten minutes after restarting, and the timeouts stopped. Checking that the vector-store container is running belongs at the top of the diagnostic list.
- **Silent `exit 1` (2026-06-13):** a separate failure class from ETIMEDOUTs, with no surviving diagnostic output and an unknown cause; if recurring, it warrants adding stderr capture to the hook script.
- **Python path-capture staleness affects standard venvs too (2026-06-17):** the `morning-briefing` pipeline's `.venv` was broken from 2026-06-12 because its `pyvenv.cfg` referenced a removed `C:\Python314`. The fix is identical in structure: rebuild against the current Python.
- **Reindex relocated to a nightly scheduled task (2026-07-27):** the heavy reindex moved into the 6:15 AM `daily-backup.ps1` task — uncapped, using the full `memsearch.exe` path, escalating per-path failures, resetting the hook timeout-streak counter on success. The session-end hook stays a light 45-second incremental pass, with its alarm threshold raised 3→6 so it fires only when the nightly safety net itself falls behind.

## Details

The Python shebang path problem in memsearch represents a distinct class of tool-configuration staleness from environment-variable and PATH issues. Unlike `setx` propagation failures or Task Scheduler PATH omissions, the memsearch issue lives in the tool's own binary: a specific file path was captured at install time and embedded in the executable. When that path ceases to exist, the binary fails at startup regardless of what the current environment looks like. The diagnostic fingerprint is: `memsearch.exe` appears to exist, its location is on PATH, but running it produces errors about Python or interpreter paths. The correct remediation is reinstallation — not PATH configuration — because the problem is inside the binary. The flush patch must be re-applied after any reinstallation, since reinstalling produces a fresh unmodified binary; the durable practice is to document the patch, reinstall cleanly, then re-apply.

The accumulated timeout findings now form a short differential diagnosis, and the 2026-09-30 result is the cautionary one: a recurring, code-shaped symptom (repeated indexing timeouts logged over several days) had a root cause entirely outside memsearch — a stopped Docker container hosting the Milvus vector store. The timeouts were real, the alarm was correct, and the tool was fine; what was down was the service it depends on. Combined with the 2026-07-27 correction, where an "occasional hiccup" was actually an hours-scale structural overrun, the pattern is that memsearch's visible failure mode (a timeout) is nearly uninformative about cause, so the diagnosis must start by checking the dependency chain — is the vector store up, is a first-time index still running, is another session holding the index — before any code is suspected. The 2026-09-30 session also confirmed that a neighboring failure in the same error log, a 2026-09-27 memory-flush failure, was a Claude usage-limit hit rather than a pipeline bug, reinforcing that a shared error log mixes resource events, quota events, and genuine defects under similar-looking lines.

The 2026-06-17 morning-briefing venv failure generalizes the Python path-capture staleness to a broader class. Both memsearch.exe (compiled binary with embedded interpreter path) and a standard `.venv` (whose `pyvenv.cfg` records `home = C:\Python314`) become non-functional when that Python is removed; the detection pattern and the fix are identical. The 2026-07-27 relocation of the heavy reindex into the nightly backup task resolved the structural case: with the hours-scale work on a nightly cadence that runs uncapped, the session-end hook is left as a light incremental pass and its consecutive-miss alarm becomes a real signal instead of chronic noise, while the full library index converges over a night or two and incremental search stays live throughout.

# Global Prompt and Hook Stack Audit (2026-09-29)

On 2026-09-29 the global prompt and hook stack was audited and repaired in a single pass: nine fixes were applied and pushed across four repos, cutting per-session startup context from roughly 17 KB to 5.7 KB while removing self-contradictory and machine-specific instructions. The user gave blanket authorization for the proposed changes rather than reviewing each one, and the work closed with a handoff at `~/Desktop/DEV/docs/handoffs/2026-09-29-prompt-audit.md`. On 2026-09-30 the audit's deliberately-deferred item — the uncleared error log — was resolved once its contents had root causes.

## Key Points

- **Error log summarized by type, not occurrence.** The startup error section now emits one line per error *type* instead of one per occurrence. This single change accounts for most of the ~17 KB → ~5.7 KB startup-context reduction, and it was also what surfaced four previously invisible error types (daily-backup ×6, perch-pull ×2, compiler-backlog ×3, and an adjudication run at 315k against a 250k token budget) that the first partial-log pass had missed.
- **A hook can neutralize a plugin's injected prompt text, but must re-apply itself.** `hooks/superpowers-quiet.mjs` strips the superpowers "MUST invoke / EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT" block at each session start. Because plugin updates overwrite plugin files, the hook re-applies the strip every session; one noisy session after any plugin update is expected. All superpowers skills remain available — only the imperative prompt block is removed.
- **Bans rewritten as goals; descriptions rewritten as instructions.** Both global instruction files were reworded from prohibitions to objectives, the session routine (pull + read STATUS at start, commit + push at end) was converted from a *description* of practice into an actual instruction, and an AGENTS.md contradiction between "output nothing" and "report errors" at startup was removed.
- **Machine-specific paths now enumerate both machines everywhere.** Vault, memory-folder, and CLI paths list both the Windows and macOS values in both machine templates plus `DEV/CLAUDE.md` and `RESEARCH.md`.
- **The error log is cleared only once its contents are explained, and only after a dated copy.** On 2026-09-29 and again the morning of 2026-09-30, `transcripts/.errors.log` was deliberately left alone — 14 KB of 9/23–9/28 failures were still unfixed, and clearing would have hidden them. Once the stack-doctor pass that day attributed the memsearch timeouts to a stopped Milvus container and the 9/27 flush failure to a usage limit, the log was cleared *after* saving a dated copy, so the next startup warning shows only new failures.
- **Trimming already-tight prose yields little.** Memory-index trimming returned only 8.4 KB → 7.7 KB against an estimate of "roughly halve," because most lines were already compressed. Structural changes (summarize by type) beat line-level editing.

## Details

The audit's most transferable result is a ranking of context-reduction tactics by yield. Rewriting the error log to summarize per error *type* collapsed a repetitive, unbounded section into a bounded one and delivered the bulk of the savings; hand-trimming the memory index recovered 0.7 KB against a predicted halving because the prose was already dense. The general lesson is that per-session context bloat usually lives in *repetition* — N occurrences of the same condition rendered N times — rather than in verbosity, so the first place to look is any section whose length scales with event count instead of with distinct state.

The error-summary rewrite also had a correctness payoff independent of size. The original pass read only part of the log and therefore missed four error types entirely; the new full-log summarizer found them. A truncating summarizer is worse than no summarizer in one specific way — it produces a short, confident-looking section that silently omits whole failure classes. The lifecycle of that log then demonstrates the complementary discipline: a warning log is a standing work queue, so clearing it is a claim that its contents are resolved. Holding it uncleared for two sessions while the failures were unexplained, then clearing it on 2026-09-30 only after each class had a root cause (Milvus container down; a usage-limit hit) and only after archiving a dated copy, preserves both properties — the next startup warning becomes a true signal about *new* failures, and nothing is actually destroyed. The dated copy is what makes clearing reversible, and therefore safe.

The `superpowers-quiet.mjs` hook establishes a pattern worth naming: a plugin that injects imperative prompt text can be muted at the consumer side without uninstalling it, by stripping the block at session start. The cost is that the fix is not durable in the plugin's own files, so the hook must re-assert itself each session — the same install-time-capture-goes-stale problem seen elsewhere in this environment, resolved here by refusing to capture at install time at all and re-deriving the desired state every session. Verification was deliberately pushed to the *next* session start rather than asserted at the end, because the fixes only take effect on a fresh read of `settings.json`. The Mac-side item could not be automated at all — the new "paths that differ" section in `machine.macos.md` must be copied by hand into the Mac's own unsynced `machine.md`.

# Connection: Numbers Right, Documentation Wrong

## The Connection

A deliverable usually carries two descriptions of itself: the computation that produced it, and a human-readable note stating what rule was applied. Verification regimes naturally test the first — recompute the cells, diff the versions, hash the staged copy — and that entire battery can pass while the second is false. Workbook 017 is the clean case: its 184-row arithmetic recompute, its 40-cell diff against 016, and the SHA-256 match between the local and staged copies all passed, and it was still blocked, because a return-only award remained in the provenance trail in contradiction of the A3 method note.

## Key Insight

The method note is a *derived artifact* with its own correctness condition, and it does not update when the implementation does. Because stakeholders read the note rather than the code, a note that overstates the implemented rule is a shipping defect with zero numerical footprint — which means no numerical check can detect it. The practical rule that follows is to put the note on the re-verification checklist whenever the rule it describes changes, and to resolve a mismatch by picking a side deliberately: either extend the code to match the note, or rewrite the note to match the code. Both were used in sequence here — Cooper DeJean was added to the exclusion list rather than the note being softened, and then the note was rewritten so its wording matched the narrower rule actually implemented.

This is the same hazard as compression distortion seen from the other end. There, a one-pager stripped the qualifiers that constrained a claim, so the summary asserted more than the source supported and corrections had to be propagated into every derived artifact rather than only the source. Here the compressed artifact is a one-cell method note rather than a one-pager, but the failure is identical in shape: the short human-readable statement is where the overstatement lives, and it is the layer the reader actually consumes. In both cases the audit that catches it is a source-level check on specific items — each newly flagged player, each numeric quotation — not an aggregate recomputation.

## Evidence

- **Workbook 017 (2026-09-30):** blocked on provenance alone. Arithmetic, version diff, and hash checks passed; the DeJean return-only award in the provenance trail contradicted the A3 note; "no current numerical effect" was recorded explicitly alongside the DO-NOT-SHIP verdict.
- **Workbook 018 (2026-09-30):** differs from 017 in exactly one cell — the A3 note — with all benchmark numbers byte-identical, and still became its own workbook number rather than an in-place edit, because the note is part of what ships.
- **Workbook 016 (2026-09-30):** the inverse lesson from the same day — "arithmetic and cached-value checks passing is not evidence the inclusion rule is right"; a source-level check on each newly flagged player is what caught the Wester defect.
- **TOS evidence brief (2026-09-18):** three numeric misquotes and a backwards Poisson argument survived into a one-pager because compression stripped the qualifiers; the remedy was propagating corrections to derived artifacts, not just fixing the source.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
